Q: Clear Edit Text - adb A:

If you use uiautomator (https://github.com/xiaocong/uiautomator), you could do this by:

  1. tap the EditText widget to get focus, then

  2. use device(focused=True).clear_text() to clear the view, or by device(focused=True).set_text("new text") to set a new text.

Q: Why did I get a segmentation fault (core dumped) error? A:

And turn on your compiler's warnings. All of them. For GCC, that would be -Wall -Wextra.
Good compilers will warn you about errors such as mismatched arguments, such as a "%d" in scanf() getting an int parameter when it expects an int *.

Then fix all the warnings. Why? Because the people who wrote the compiler that you're using to translate your code into an executable took extra time to tell you they think your code is dodgy. Read that again: the people who wrote the compiler you're using took extra time to tell you your code is dodgy. You probably should listen to the experts who wrote the tool you're using when they put extra effort in to tell you your code is dodgy.

Q: How to revert the SVN trunk and put it in a branch? A:

Is there a 'normal' way to do this in svn?

Yes, there is. Please, read the documentation:

  • SVN MergeBook
  • SVNBook | Branching and Merging.

Generally speaking there are several different approaches, but I would try the following:

  1. Undo revision 1082 and commit this change to the repository. Read Undoing Changes.
  2. Create a branch out of trunk. Read Creating a Branch.
  3. Run cherry-pick merge to copy revision 1081 to the new branch. Read Cherrypicking.

Q: Getting Initials from a name in R A:

You can also use the abbreviate function.

> NAMES <- data.frame(ID = "George Washington")
> NAMES$ID <- as.character(NAMES$ID)
> abbreviate(NAMES$ID, minlength = 2)
George Washington 
             "GW"

Q: A svn branch is a full copy of trunk files or just a link? A:

Subversion uses cheap copies. You can consider copy / branch or tag as a link. See Cheap Copies section in SVNBook | Using Branches and SVN MergeBook | Branches.

Q: How SVN store branch on the server? A:

SVNBook | Using Branches tells us (check the "Cheap Copies" part):

Subversion's repository has a special design. When you copy a directory, you don't need to worry about the repository growing huge—Subversion doesn't actually duplicate any data. Instead, it creates a new directory entry that points to an existing tree. If you're an experienced Unix user, you'll recognize this as the same concept behind a hard link. As further changes are made to files and directories beneath the copied directory, Subversion continues to employ this hard link concept where it can. It duplicates data only when it is necessary to disambiguate different versions of objects.

And see SVN MergeBook as well: https://www.axiorema.com/docs/subversion/latest/branching-and-merging/concepts/branches/

Q: Hashing a dictionary? A:

How to hash a dictionary in Python

Quick summary

hash_input_str = json.dumps(my_dict, sort_keys=True, default=str)
hash_hex_str = hashlib.sha256(hash_input_str.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

Details

Building on the main answer, it's best to also set default=str. This passes in the str() built-in function to convert otherwise non-serializable objects to string representations for the json dump. This is important because some objects (like datetime or Decimal) are not JSON serializable by default.

If you run json.dumps() on a dictionary with such a non-serializable object, it will raise a TypeError like this:

TypeError: Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable

So, here's the best way to stringify a dictionary for hashing:

hash_input_str = json.dumps(my_dict, sort_keys=True, default=str)

The sort_keys=True ensures that the keys are sorted, which is important for consistent hashing. The default=str argument automatically tries to call str() on any object that isn't otherwise serializable by default.

Then you can hash it like this:

hash_hex_str = hashlib.sha256(hash_input_str.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

Full, runnable example:

hash_a_dict.py from my eRCaGuy_hello_world repo:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import hashlib
import json
import datetime

my_dict = {
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 30,
    "balance": 1234.56,  # Decimal or float
    "timestamp": datetime.datetime.now()  # Non-serializable object
}

hash_input_str = json.dumps(my_dict, sort_keys=True, default=str)
hash_hex_str = hashlib.sha256(hash_input_str.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

print(f"my_dict:               {my_dict}")
print(f"Hashable input string: {hash_input_str}")
print(f"SHA256 hash:           {hash_hex_str}")

Example run and output:

eRCaGuy_hello_world$ python/hash_a_dict.py
my_dict:               {'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 30, 'balance': 1234.56, 'timestamp': datetime.datetime(2026, 8, 19, 11, 55, 29, 432634)}
Hashable input string: {"age": 30, "balance": 1234.56, "name": "John Doe", "timestamp": "2026-08-19 11:55:29.432634"}
SHA256 hash:           5b06f921ea9d78b435809155ce33831d883393e09f9789524793ffff2691e5f2

Going further: filter out certain keys from the dictionary before hashing

To avoid hashing a certain key, such as the timestamp, filter it out first like this:

my_dict_filtered = {key: value for key, value in my_dict.items() if key != "timestamp"}
hash_input_str_filtered = json.dumps(my_dict_filtered, sort_keys=True, default=str)
hash_hex_str_filtered = hashlib.sha256(hash_input_str_filtered.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

References

  1. The main answer here
  2. json.dumps() docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.dumps
  3. json.dump() docs to explain the args for json.dumps(): https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.dump
  4. hashlib.sha256() docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html#hashlib.sha256
